notes.meaning: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon marched to Jerusalem and surrounded it in the third year of King Jehoiakim of Judah. This siege began the exile of God's people away from their homeland. The Lord used this foreign king to carry out his warnings against Judah's unfaithfulness.

The Lord allowed King Jehoiakim and some holy objects from the temple to fall into Nebuchadnezzar's power. The conqueror carried these sacred treasures to Babylon and put them into the treasure house of his own god. Judah fell not because Babylon's idols were stronger than the true God, but because the Lord himself handed them over as discipline.

Nebuchadnezzar commanded his chief palace officer, Ashpenaz, to bring in a group of young men from Israel's royal family and nobility. The king wanted talented captives whom he could train to work in his royal court. This action fulfilled an earlier prophecy that royal sons of Judah would become servants in Babylon's palace.

The king selected youths who had healthy, handsome bodies and sharp, capable minds. They were to spend three years studying the difficult language, history, and science of the Babylonians. Nebuchadnezzar wanted to educate these young men so they could serve effectively as high-ranking officials in his empire.

The king ordered that these young men be fed every day with the same fine food and wine served at his own table. Their royal training was to last for three years before they entered palace service. This generous provision was meant to win their loyalty and make them fully comfortable with Babylonian life.

Among the noble captives chosen from the tribe of Judah were Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. These four are named because their deep faith and courageous choices form the heart of what follows. God brought them to Babylon to be his witnesses during a dark period of exile.

The chief official gave each of the four youths a new Babylonian name: Belteshazzar, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. Their original Hebrew names honored the true God, but their new names honored Babylonian idols. This change was meant to make them forget their homeland and fit into pagan culture, though their inner faith remained unchanged.

Daniel resolved in his heart that he would not make himself unclean by eating the king's royal food or drinking his wine. The palace meat likely broke God's dietary laws or had been dedicated to pagan gods in idol worship. Even as a young captive far from home, Daniel respectfully asked permission to remain pure before the Lord.

God caused the chief official to feel genuine kindness and sympathy toward Daniel. Even though Daniel was a prisoner of war, the Lord quietly worked in the official's heart to protect him. God often prepares the way for his people when they seek to obey him in difficult places.

The chief official explained that he feared the king, who had personally ordered their daily meals. He worried that if Daniel and his friends ended up looking thinner or less healthy than the other youths, the king would have him put to death. His reply showed that he liked Daniel, but he could not risk his own life against an absolute ruler.

Daniel turned to the steward whom the chief official had placed directly in charge of their daily care. Since the top official was too afraid to give permission, Daniel pursued a practical alternative with the man who actually served their meals. Wisdom often means seeking another safe and polite path when the first door closes.

Daniel asked the steward to test the four of them for ten days on a simple diet of vegetables and water. Eating plain food grown from seed would keep them from breaking God's laws or taking part in idol worship. It was a humble step of faith that trusted God to sustain their physical strength.

Daniel urged the steward to compare their health with the other youths after the ten days were up. He promised that the steward could then decide what to do based on the clear results. Daniel acted with gentle courtesy and complete confidence that God would protect them.

The steward agreed to the proposal and put the four young men on trial for ten days. Ten days was short enough to avoid any immediate danger with the king while testing whether the simple diet would work. God used Daniel's reasonable and respectful request to win the guard's cooperation.

At the end of the ten days, the four young men looked healthier, stronger, and better nourished than all the youths eating the rich food from the king's table. Their radiant health was a direct result of God's blessing on their obedience rather than just a natural diet. God showed that true well-being comes from his hand.

The steward saw the positive outcome and took away the king's rich food and wine for good, serving them vegetables instead. This allowed the young men to follow God's laws freely throughout their entire training period. It also benefited the steward, who could keep the valuable palace meals for his own family.

God gave all four young men outstanding ability to master literature, philosophy, and practical wisdom. On top of that, the Lord gave Daniel the special spiritual gift of interpreting all kinds of dreams and visions. While all four succeeded in their studies, Daniel was equipped by God to act as a prophet in a pagan royal court.

When the three-year training period ended, Ashpenaz brought all the educated youths before King Nebuchadnezzar for their final evaluation. The king personally inspected every candidate to see how much they had learned. This oral exam was the crucial step before receiving an official appointment in the palace.

The king questioned all the candidates and found no one who matched Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. Because of their remarkable character and clear understanding, they entered directly into the king's royal service. God rewarded their steadfast loyalty by placing them in positions of great influence.

Whenever the king consulted these four young men on difficult matters requiring wisdom and good judgment, he found them ten times better than all his magicians and astrologers. Babylon leaned heavily on occult advisors and soothsayers, but God's gift of truth far outshone all pagan magic. The Lord proved his superiority right at the heart of the world's most powerful empire.

Daniel continued in his palace service until the first year of King Cyrus of Persia, when the exile began to end. This note does not mean he died that year, since he received later visions, but that he outlived the entire Babylonian empire. Human kingdoms rise and fall, but God preserves his faithful servants through every change.
